english: Tell me about it / I know, right? / Exactly what I was thinking (strong, sympathetic agreement)
usage: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 딱 그 생각 했어요.
Tell me about it — I was thinking the exact same thing.
Agreeing and confirming you felt it too
그러게 말이야, 진짜 너무하지 않아?
I know, right? Isn't it just too much?
그러게 말이야 = casual form with friends
그러게나 말이에요.
Yeah, you can say that again.
그러게나 = slightly stronger/heavier sigh
그러게 말입니다.
Indeed, you're quite right.
-ㅂ니다 form, polite to a senior or at work
examples: A: 요즘 물가가 너무 올랐어요. B: 그러게 말이에요.
A: Prices have shot up lately. B: Tell me about it.
Bare reaction — just the agreement, nothing added
A: 주말마다 비가 오네요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 빨래를 못 하겠어요.
A: It rains every weekend. B: I know, right? I can't even do laundry.
Agreement + you pile on your own grievance
A: 그 사람 진짜 일을 잘하더라고요. B: 그러게 말이에요, 저도 보고 깜짝 놀랐어요.
A: That person is really good at their job. B: Right? I was honestly surprised when I saw it.
Works for a positive remark too, not only complaints
nuance: Whole-hearted, sympathetic agreement that means far more than a flat 네 or 맞아요 — it carries the extra charge 'and I've felt exactly that myself.' Built from 그러게 ('right, isn't it') plus 말이에요 (literally 'it is [my] words'), it's the heavier, more emphatic cousin of plain 그러게요: where 그러게요 is a quick nod, 그러게 말이에요 is a shared sigh that says 'you took the words out of my mouth.' Contrast it with 맞아요, which simply confirms a fact ('that's correct'); 그러게 말이에요 instead bonds you emotionally over a shared feeling, usually a complaint or a 'what can you do' resignation. It is casual-polite (해요체); drop to 그러게 말이야 with close friends and go up to 그러게 말입니다 with a boss. The English-speaker pitfall: don't reach for it to accept a compliment about yourself ('You're so good!' → 그러게 말이에요 sounds like you're agreeing you're great) — it only mirrors the other person's observation, so reserve it for things you both perceive from the outside.

mistakes: English speakers use it to accept praise ('You did great!' → 그러게 말이에요), which sounds like smug self-agreement. It's only for echoing a remark about something you both see, not about yourself — for praise say 감사합니다 instead.
It only confirms what was just said, so don't follow it with a counter-argument. To agree-then-disagree you need 그건 그런데… ('that's true, but…'), not 그러게 말이에요.
Don't shorten it to just 말이에요 hoping to keep the meaning — without 그러게 it just means 'I'm telling you / it's true,' losing the empathetic-agreement function.

english: No, that's not it — / It's not that, it's… / What I mean is… (correcting a misunderstanding)
usage: 그게 아니라, 제 말은 좀 다른 뜻이었어요.
No, that's not it — what I meant was a bit different.
Clarifying after being misunderstood
아니 그게 아니라, 시간이 없어서 그래.
No no, it's not that — it's because I don't have time.
그게 아니라 = casual; correcting a wrong assumption
그런 게 아니라 그냥 좀 피곤해서요.
It's not like that, I'm just a bit tired.
그런 게 아니라 = 'it's not that kind of thing'
그게 아니고, 다시 설명할게요.
That's not it — let me explain again.
그게 아니고 = looser spoken variant
examples: A: 이거 싫어요? B: 그게 아니라 배가 불러서요.
A: You don't like this? B: It's not that — I'm just full.
Short, two-clause correction
A: 저 싫어서 안 오시는 거예요? B: 아, 그게 아니라 오늘 진짜 바빠서 그래요.
A: Are you not coming because you don't like me? B: Oh, that's not it — it's just that I'm really busy today.
Heading off a hurt feeling before it lands
A: 환불해 달라는 거죠? B: 그게 아니라 사실은 교환을 하고 싶어서 말씀드린 거예요.
A: So you want a refund? B: No — actually I brought it up because I'd like an exchange.
Real-situation correction of a misread request
nuance: An everyday repair phrase you fire off the instant someone misreads your words or your motive: literally '그게 (that) + 아니라 (it is not, and so…).' The 아니라 form is the connective of 아니다 ('to not be'), so the phrase is grammatically unfinished on purpose — it leans forward into the correct version that must follow. Leading with 그게 아니라 softens a correction the way English 'no, what I mean is…' does: you're fixing a misunderstanding, not winning an argument, so it protects the other person's face. Distinguish it carefully from 그게 아니면, which sounds nearly identical but means 'if not that, then…' and offers an alternative rather than denying; and from 그런 게 아니라 ('it's not that kind of thing'), which denies a whole category rather than one specific claim. It rides any speech level — add 요 (그게 아니라요) for extra politeness. The pitfall for English speakers: treating it as a standalone 'No.' Korean expects the true statement attached right after, or you sound like you cut yourself off.

Saying 그것이 아니라 in casual speech sounds stiff and bookish; the natural spoken contraction is 그게 아니라. Reserve the full 그것이 for formal writing.

english: Now that you mention it / Come to think of it / Now that I think about it (realizing something mid-conversation)
usage: 그러고 보니 오늘 점심을 안 먹었네요.
Come to think of it, I haven't eaten lunch today.
Realizing something as you speak
그러고 보니까 너 머리 잘랐네?
Now that I look — did you get a haircut?
그러고 보니까 = -까 adds a casual 'now that…'
그러고 보니 벌써 12월이네요.
Now that you mention it, it's already December.
Noticing how time has passed
듣고 보니 그러네요.
Now that I hear it, you're right.
Related: 듣고 보니 = 'now that I've heard it'
examples: 그러고 보니 우산을 안 가져왔네.
Come to think of it, I didn't bring an umbrella.
Simple solo realization, one clause
A: 민수 씨 요즘 안 보이네요. B: 그러고 보니 진짜 한참 못 봤네요.
A: I haven't seen Minsu lately. B: Now that you mention it, it really has been a while.
Triggered by what the other person just said
그러고 보니 우리 처음 만난 지 벌써 일 년이나 됐네요, 시간 참 빠르다.
Now that I think about it, it's already been a whole year since we first met — time really flies.
Real reflection, spun out into a fuller thought
nuance: A connector for the exact moment a thought clicks into place. It breaks down as 그러고 ('having done/been so') + 보니 ('upon looking,' the -고 보니 'do and then realize' pattern), so literally 'looking at it that way, I now notice…' — the realization is fresh, sparked by what someone just said or by something you glanced at. Compare 그러고 보니 with 알고 보니 ('as it turns out / on closer inspection it was actually…'), which reveals a hidden truth, and with 듣고 보니 ('now that I've heard it'), which is specifically prompted by hearing the other person out; 그러고 보니 is the broadest 'huh, now that I consider it.' The form is identical across speech levels — only the verb ending that follows changes (보니 오늘…네요 vs …네). Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, it marks NEW awareness, so don't use it for facts you already knew. Second, watch the spacing and spelling — 그러고 (from 그러다) is not 그리고 ('and'); a single vowel flips the whole meaning, and it stays two words: 그러고 보니.

english: Maybe that's why / Perhaps because of that / That might be why (guessing a cause)
usage: 어제 잠을 못 잤어요. 그래서 그런지 하루 종일 피곤하네요.
I couldn't sleep last night. Maybe that's why I'm tired all day.
Linking a likely cause to a result
주말이라 그런지 사람이 진짜 많네.
Maybe because it's the weekend, there are so many people.
N(이)라 그런지 = 'perhaps because it's N'
비가 와서 그런지 길이 한산해요.
Perhaps because it's raining, the streets are quiet.
V/A-아서 그런지 = 'maybe because ~'
요즘 운동을 해서 그런지 컨디션이 좋아요.
Maybe it's because I've been exercising — I feel great lately.
Crediting a habit for a good result
examples: 피곤해서 그런지 자꾸 하품이 나와요.
Maybe because I'm tired, I keep yawning.
One cause, one observed result
A: 오늘따라 가게가 한가하네요. B: 평일이라 그런지 손님이 별로 없어요.
A: The shop's unusually quiet today. B: Maybe because it's a weekday, there aren't many customers.
Speculating about a cause in dialogue
새 안경을 바꿔서 그런지 눈이 좀 피곤하고 머리도 살짝 아프네요.
Maybe because I changed to new glasses, my eyes feel tired and my head aches a little too.
Tentative self-diagnosis, two symptoms
nuance: A soft, speculative cause-marker meaning 'I suspect this is the reason, though I'm not certain.' The key is the -ㄴ지 ending (from 그렇다, 'to be so'): 그런지 literally asks-to-itself 'whether it's so,' which is what bakes in the hedge. So 그래서 그런지 = 'so, [maybe] because of that…,' pointing back to a reason you just gave, while -아서/어서 그런지 and -(이)라 그런지 attach the guess directly onto a cause ('because it rained, perhaps…' / 'because it's the weekend, perhaps…'). The sharp contrast to learn is against bare 그래서 ('so, therefore'), which states a cause you're SURE of: 비가 와서 길이 막혀요 ('it's raining so traffic is jammed' — definite) versus 비가 와서 그런지 길이 막히네요 ('maybe because it's raining, traffic seems jammed' — tentative observation). Using plain 그래서 when you're only guessing sounds overconfident; using 그래서 그런지 when the cause is obvious sounds oddly wishy-washy. It describes an observed result, so the English-speaker trap is trying to bolt a command or request onto it (그래서 그런지 + '…please do X') — it can only end in a statement of what you noticed.

english: Anyway / By the way / That aside (changing the subject)
usage: 그건 그렇고, 점심 뭐 먹을까요?
Anyway, what should we eat for lunch?
Pivoting to a new topic
그건 그렇고 너 요즘 회사는 어때?
By the way, how's work these days?
Casual subject change with a friend
그건 그렇다 치고, 다음 얘기 해요.
Setting that aside, let's move on.
그건 그렇다 치고 = 'granting that, anyway'
그나저나 시간 괜찮으세요?
Anyway, do you have time?
그나저나 = a close synonym for switching topics
examples: 그건 그렇고, 너 밥은 먹었어?
Anyway, did you eat?
Quick pivot to a new question
A: 그 드라마 결말이 좀 아쉬웠어요. B: 그러게요. 그건 그렇고, 주말에 시간 돼요?
A: That drama's ending was a bit disappointing. B: Right. Anyway, are you free this weekend?
Close one topic, open a fresh one
회의 보고는 잘 끝났어요. 그건 그렇고, 아까 말씀하신 그 책 제목이 뭐였죠?
The meeting report wrapped up fine. By the way, what was the title of that book you mentioned earlier?
Real situation: park business, reopen an earlier thread
nuance: A friendly topic-switcher that literally says 'that — that's so, and…' (그건 = 그것은 'that thing' contracted; 그렇고 = 그렇다 'to be so' + connective -고). It gently certifies the current topic as settled ('right, that's how it is') before swinging to a new one, which is why it never feels abrupt — you're acknowledging, not dropping. Compare three neighbors: 그건 그렇고 closes a topic to open any new one; 그나저나 ('anyway / be that as it may') is an almost interchangeable swap with the same easy register; but 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it's come up') does the OPPOSITE — it segues to a RELATED point rather than away to a new one. So if the next thing connects, use 말이 나왔으니까; if you're leaving the subject behind, use 그건 그렇고. It's casual-polite and extremely common in speech. Pitfalls for English speakers: don't deploy it to disagree — 'by the way' in English can preface a jab, but 그건 그렇고 only steers topics, never pushes back. And mind the spelling: it's 그건 (one contracted word) 그렇고, and 그렇고 keeps the ㅎ (don't write 그러고, which is a different verb).

Spelling 그렇고 as 그러고. 그렇고 comes from 그렇다 ('to be so') and keeps the ㅎ; 그러고 comes from 그러다 ('to do so') and means something else. Different verb, different meaning.
Using it to introduce a closely RELATED follow-up. If the new remark grows out of the same topic, the natural choice is 말이 나왔으니까 ('since it came up'); 그건 그렇고 implies you're leaving the topic behind.

english: Since we're on the subject / Now that it's come up / Speaking of which (segueing into a related point)
usage: 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데, 저도 그게 좀 불편했어요.
Since it's come up, I'll say it — that bothered me a little too.
말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 = set lead-in to a frank remark
말 나온 김에 지금 정하자.
Since we're already on it, let's decide now.
말 나온 김에 = shorter, casual variant
여행 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 다음에 같이 갈래요?
Speaking of travel — want to go together next time?
Tacking onto a topic that just arose
돈 얘기가 나왔으니까 솔직히 말할게요.
Since money came up, I'll be honest.
얘기가 나왔으니까 = 'since the talk came up'
examples: 말이 나왔으니까 하나만 더 물어볼게요.
Since it's come up, let me ask just one more thing.
Short segue into a single follow-up question
A: 회식은 다음 주 금요일이에요. B: 아, 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 저는 그날 좀 늦을 것 같아요.
A: The team dinner is next Friday. B: Oh, since it's come up — I'll probably be a bit late that day.
Adding relevant info while the topic is open
이사 말이 나왔으니까 말인데, 혹시 그 동네에 괜찮은 집 있으면 좀 소개해 줄 수 있어요?
Speaking of moving — if you happen to know a decent place in that neighborhood, could you put me onto it?
Real situation: ride the topic into a polite request
nuance: A spoken segue that piggybacks on a topic someone just raised so your follow-up feels invited rather than out of nowhere. It parses as 말이 ('the topic/word,' subject) + 나왔으니까 (나오다 'to come out' in past + -(으)니까 'since/because'), i.e. 'since the subject has come out.' The fuller, very idiomatic 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it's come up, this is what I'll say…') typically front-loads a candid opinion or a small request, cushioning it. Two contrasts sharpen its use: against 그건 그렇고, which switches AWAY to an unrelated topic — 말이 나왔으니까 instead leans INTO the current one; and against the casual cousin 말 나온 김에 (using -(으)ㄴ 김에 'while we're at it'), which stresses convenient timing ('as long as we're on it, let's do it now') more than the candid-remark flavor. Casual-polite, and you can shorten to 말 나온 김에 with friends. The English-speaker pitfall: 'speaking of which…' in English can pivot to anything loosely associated, but 말이 나왔으니까 demands a genuinely related thread that JUST surfaced — for an unrelated jump, you need 그건 그렇고. And like the other lead-ins here, it's incomplete on its own; the real point must follow.

The fuller, very idiomatic 말이 나왔으니까 하는 말인데 ('since it's come up, this is what I'll say…') typically front-loads a candid opinion or a small request, cushioning it. Casual-polite, and you can shorten to 말 나온 김에 with friends. Like the other lead-ins here, it's incomplete on its own; the real point must follow.

Two contrasts sharpen its use: against 그건 그렇고, which switches AWAY to an unrelated topic — 말이 나왔으니까 instead leans INTO the current one; and against the casual cousin 말 나온 김에 (using -(으)ㄴ 김에 'while we're at it'), which stresses convenient timing ('as long as we're on it, let's do it now') more than the candid-remark flavor.
It parses as 말이 ('the topic/word,' subject) + 나왔으니까 (나오다 'to come out' in past + -(으)니까 'since/because'), i.e. 'since the subject has come out.'
'Speaking of which…' in English can pivot to anything loosely associated, but 말이 나왔으니까 demands a genuinely related thread that JUST surfaced — for an unrelated jump, you need 그건 그렇고.

mistakes: Using it to jump to an unrelated topic, the way English 'speaking of which' can drift. 말이 나왔으니까 requires the point to be genuinely tied to what just came up; for an unrelated switch use 그건 그렇고.
Leaving it dangling as if it were a full sentence. It's a lead-in — you must follow it with the actual remark or request (often via …말인데, …할게요, …물어볼게요).
Mis-conjugating 나오다: it's 나왔으니까 (past + 으니까), not 나오니까. The topic has ALREADY come up, so the past tense is what makes the 'now that it's surfaced' meaning work.

english: Oh good / What a relief / I'm glad to hear that (relieved that things turned out okay)
usage: 다 잘 끝났다니 다행이네요.
I'm glad to hear it all worked out.
Reacting with relief to good news
안 다쳤다니 정말 다행이다.
Thank goodness you weren't hurt.
다행이다 = casual; 정말 adds weight
불행 중 다행이에요.
It's a blessing in disguise / could've been worse.
불행 중 다행 = set phrase, 'fortunate amid misfortune'
늦지 않아서 다행이에요.
Good thing we weren't late.
V/A-아서 다행이다 = 'lucky that ~'
examples: A: 시험 통과했어요. B: 아, 다행이네요.
A: I passed the exam. B: Oh, what a relief.
Bare relief reaction to good news
A: 검사 결과 괜찮대요. B: 아, 다행이네요. 저도 걱정 많이 했어요.
A: The test results are fine. B: Oh, what a relief. I was really worried too.
Relief on someone else's behalf, with a reason
가방에 있을 줄은 몰랐어요. 진짜 잃어버린 줄 알고 한참 찾았는데, 있어서 정말 다행이에요.
I had no idea it was in my bag. I really thought I'd lost it and searched for ages — I'm so relieved it turned up.
Real situation: relief after a genuine scare
nuance: A warm, sincere reaction of relief. The core noun is Sino-Korean 다행 (多幸), literally 'much (多) good fortune (幸),' so the phrase means 'how fortunate' rather than just 'good.' Aimed at someone else's news it reads as caring ('I'm relieved FOR you'); about your own situation it's a heartfelt 'phew.' The -네요 ending (해요체) adds spontaneous, in-the-moment warmth — a beat more emotional than the flatter 다행이에요. Don't confuse this relief word with two near neighbors: 잘됐네요 ('that turned out well / good for you') celebrates a positive OUTCOME you're happy about, whereas 다행이에요 specifically exhales relief that something bad was AVOIDED; and 축하해요 ('congratulations') honors an achievement someone earned, not a near-miss they survived. Casual form is 다행이다 with friends. The classic English-speaker pitfall is the spelling slip 다행이네요 vs 다행히: 다행이네요 uses the NOUN 다행 + 이다, but 다행히 is the ADVERB 'fortunately' (다행히 늦지 않았어요, 'fortunately we weren't late') and can't end a sentence as a reaction. Mixing them produces ungrammatical Korean.

Saying 다행이네요 about a trivial non-event where nothing was ever at risk. The word implies there WAS a worry or danger that has now passed — without that tension it sounds odd.

english: Oh no, this is bad / We're in trouble / Uh-oh, big problem (reacting to something going wrong)
usage: 큰일 났다, 지갑을 집에 두고 왔어.
Oh no, I left my wallet at home.
Realizing a problem; casual
어떡해요, 큰일 났어요.
What do I do, this is a disaster.
큰일 났어요 = polite; pairs with 어떡해요
이러다 큰일 나겠다.
At this rate something bad's going to happen.
큰일 나다 (future) = 'trouble will happen'
큰일 날 뻔했어요.
That was a close call — could've been a disaster.
큰일 날 뻔하다 = 'nearly went wrong'
examples: 큰일 났어, 늦었어!
Oh no, I'm late!
Two-word alarm in the heat of the moment
A: 기차 막차 끊겼대요. B: 헐, 큰일 났네요.
A: They say the last train's gone. B: Oh no, we're in trouble.
Reacting to bad news together
발표 자료를 USB에 안 넣어 왔어, 이거 진짜 큰일 났다, 어떡하지?
I didn't load the presentation onto the USB — this is seriously bad, what do I do?
Real situation: genuine panic at a mistake
nuance: A high-alarm reaction that literally says 'a big thing (큰일) has happened (났다).' 큰일 is 큰 ('big') + 일 ('matter/affair'), and 났다 is the past of 나다 ('to occur/break out'), so the whole thing is 'a major affair has broken out' — fired off the moment you realize something's gone wrong or is about to. Tone runs the full range from real panic to a half-joking 'uh-oh.' Mind the tense, because it shifts the meaning: 큰일 났다/났어 (past) = trouble has ALREADY landed; 큰일 나다 in future/conditional (이러다 큰일 나겠다, 큰일 날 뻔했다) warns of trouble LOOMING or narrowly dodged. Contrast it with the gentler 어쩌나 ('oh dear, what to do'), which is soft, sympathetic worry usually on someone ELSE's behalf, whereas 큰일 났다 is an urgent alarm about a concrete problem, often your own. Casual as 큰일 났다/났어; polite as 큰일 났어요, and it loves pairing with 어떡해 ('what do I do'). Two pitfalls: keep 큰일 as ONE noun (write 큰일 났다, not 큰 일 났다 as separate words in this fixed expression), and don't fire it at trivial inconveniences — it implies a real problem, even when you're exaggerating for comic effect.

Using the past 큰일 났다 for trouble that hasn't happened yet. For looming danger use the future/conditional: 이러다 큰일 나겠다 ('something bad's going to happen at this rate') or 큰일 날 뻔했다 ('almost went wrong').

Deploying it for minor annoyances (a small typo, a tiny delay). It implies a genuinely serious problem; overusing it for trifles makes you sound melodramatic. For small hiccups, 어떡하지 or 아 이런 fits better.

english: Oh no, what to do / Oh dear / How awful (sympathetic worry, often on someone's behalf)
usage: 아이고, 어쩌나.
Oh dear, what to do.
아이고 + 어쩌나 = classic worried reaction
이를 어쩌나, 표가 다 매진이네.
Oh no, what now — the tickets are all sold out.
이를 어쩌나 = 'what to do about this'
어쩌나 했는데 잘 풀렸어요.
I was worried, but it sorted itself out.
어쩌나 했는데 = 'I was anxious, but…'
혼자 가야 한다니 어쩌니.
You have to go alone? Oh dear.
어쩌니 = softer/older-sounding variant
examples: 어쩌나, 비 오는데.
Oh no, and it's raining.
Short sympathetic murmur
A: 감기가 안 낫네요. B: 어쩌나, 병원은 가 보셨어요?
A: My cold won't go away. B: Oh no — have you seen a doctor?
Sympathy for someone, then a caring question
면접에 늦으면 어쩌나 싶어서 새벽부터 조마조마했어요.
I was on edge since dawn, fretting over what I'd do if I were late to the interview.
Real situation: 어쩌나 embedded as 'worried that ~'
nuance: A soft exclamation of worry or tenderness — 'oh dear, what's to be done.' It contracts from 어찌하나 ('how shall [I/we] do it'): 어찌 ('how') + 하다 ('do') + the musing -나 ending, which is a question you murmur to yourself rather than ask out loud. That self-directed quality is why it lands as a feeling, not a real request for instructions. It can stand alone as a reaction or nest inside a sentence ('…ㄹ까 봐 / …면 어쩌나 싶다' = 'worried that…'). The crucial contrast is with 큰일 났다: 큰일 났다 is loud alarm about a concrete problem, often your own, while 어쩌나 is gentler, warmer, and typically aimed at SOMEONE ELSE's predicament — concern, not panic. Its near-synonym 어쩌지 leans toward your OWN dilemma ('what should I do?'), whereas 어쩌나 more often sighs over another person's plight; 어쩌니 is a softer, slightly old-fashioned color. The pitfall for English speakers: because it LOOKS like a question (and even ends like one), learners answer it or use it to actually solicit advice. It isn't a genuine question — it's an empathetic sigh. If you truly want guidance, ask 어떻게 하죠? or 어떡하면 좋을까요?

Aiming it at someone as criticism ('어쩌나' with a blaming tone). It conveys sympathy and worry, never reproach — pointing it accusingly at a person misreads the warmth built into it.
Confusing 어쩌나 (soft worry, often for others) with 어쩌지 (your own 'what should I do'). They overlap, but 어쩌지 fits self-directed indecision better, while 어쩌나 suits sighing over another's trouble.

english: That can happen / It's possible, I guess / Fair enough (accepting something as understandable)
usage: 뭐, 그럴 수도 있죠.
Well, that can happen, I suppose.
Accepting something gracefully
그럴 수도 있지, 누구나 실수하잖아.
That can happen — everyone makes mistakes.
그럴 수도 있지 = casual, reassuring
바쁘면 그럴 수도 있어요.
If you're busy, that's understandable.
Excusing someone's lapse
그럴 수도 있겠네요.
I suppose that could be the case.
Conceding a point as plausible
examples: A: 제가 길을 잘못 들었어요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠.
A: I took the wrong road. B: That happens.
Short, easygoing absolution
A: 그 사람이 오해했나 봐요. B: 그럴 수도 있죠, 설명이 좀 부족했으니까요.
A: I think they misunderstood. B: That's possible — the explanation was a bit lacking.
Conceding a reasonable point with a reason
A: 제가 깜빡하고 답장을 못 했어요, 죄송해요. B: 괜찮아요, 그럴 수도 있죠, 바쁘셨을 텐데요 뭐.
A: I forgot to reply, I'm sorry. B: It's fine, that happens — you must've been busy.
Real situation: warmly waving off a small slip
nuance: An easygoing, generous phrase meaning 'that falls within the range of normal — no big deal.' It's built from 그렇다 ('to be so') → 그럴 (prospective modifier) + 수도 있다 ('there's even the possibility'), with 수 being the bound noun for 'possibility/ability,' so literally 'there could even be such a case.' The -죠 (from -지요) ending fishes for soft mutual agreement — 'right?' — which is what makes it sound understanding rather than declarative. Its job is to forgive a minor mistake, validate a feeling, or grant that a possibility is reasonable, making it the warm opposite of 말도 안 돼요 ('that makes no sense / no way'). Draw a sharp line against the near-twin 그럴 리가 없죠: identical rhythm, opposite meaning — 그럴 수도 있죠 ACCEPTS that something is possible/understandable, while 그럴 리가 없죠 DENIES it ('there's no way that's true'). One 수 vs 리 flips acceptance into disbelief. Casual as 그럴 수도 있지. The English-speaker pitfall: because it signals 'understandable, no harm done,' don't aim it at something genuinely serious — replying 그럴 수도 있죠 to a real grievance or a big mistake sounds flippant and dismissive, as if you're shrugging off something that actually matters.

Spacing 그럴 수도 as 그럴수도. 수 is a bound noun and stays a separate word: 그럴 수도 있죠. Writing it joined is a common orthography slip.

english: I think that'd be best / You'd better do that / That sounds like the way to go (gently recommending)
usage: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
Yes, I think that'd be best.
Agreeing that a suggested course is wise
피곤하면 좀 쉬는 게 좋겠어.
If you're tired, you'd better rest a bit.
V-는 게 좋겠다 = 'had better ~'; casual
미리 예약하는 게 좋겠어요.
It'd be best to book in advance.
Recommending a sensible step
그러지 않는 게 좋겠어요.
I don't think you should do that.
Negative form = gentle 'better not'
examples: 그게 좋겠어요.
That would be best.
Bare endorsement of an idea on the table
A: 의사한테 한번 물어볼까요? B: 네, 그러는 게 좋겠어요.
A: Should I ask the doctor? B: Yes, that'd be the way to go.
Backing a wise action someone proposed
내일 아침 일찍 출발해야 하니까, 오늘은 일찍 자는 게 좋겠어요.
Since we have to leave early tomorrow morning, you'd better get to sleep early tonight.
Real situation: caring advice anchored to a reason
nuance: A polite, gentle recommendation. The engine is the pattern V-는 게 좋겠다 — 는 게 (from 는 것이, 'the act of doing') + 좋겠다 ('would be good'), literally 'it'd be good if [you/we] did ~,' i.e. English 'had better' or 'I think you should.' The all-important -겠- is a softener of supposition here, downgrading a bare fact (좋다, 'is good') into a tentative 'would (probably) be good,' so you advise without bossing. 그러는 게 좋겠어요 specifically endorses a course ALREADY raised in the conversation ('yes — doing that would be best'), with 그러다 ('to do so') standing in for the action just mentioned. Two contrasts matter. First, against the blunt command V-(으)세요 ('do it'): 예약하세요 orders, while 예약하는 게 좋겠어요 merely advises — choosing the imperative where advice is expected can sound pushy to a peer. Second, against V-는 게 어때요? ('how about doing ~?'), which OFFERS an option and leaves the decision open, whereas -는 게 좋겠어요 states your considered RECOMMENDATION. Casual form is 그러는 게 좋겠어. English-speaker pitfalls: don't translate 'you'd better' with its English threat-flavor — Korean -는 게 좋겠어요 is soft, not a warning; and keep the spacing 그러는 게 (게 = 것이 contracted) as a separate word.

english: Do as you like / Suit yourself / It's up to you (giving free rein — or, with a cold tone, 'fine, whatever')
usage: 편하실 대로 마음대로 하세요.
Please do whatever's comfortable for you.
Warm version — genuinely leaving it to them
네 마음대로 해.
Do whatever you want.
마음대로 해 = casual; tone decides if it's kind or curt
마음껏 드세요.
Help yourself, eat as much as you like.
마음껏 = 'to your heart's content' (friendly cousin)
그럼 마음대로 하든가.
Then do whatever you want, see if I care.
-든가 makes it pointedly cold/annoyed
examples: A: 여기 앉아도 돼요? B: 네, 마음대로 하세요.
A: Can I sit here? B: Sure, go right ahead.
Short, friendly permission
메뉴는 마음대로 고르세요, 오늘은 제가 살게요.
Order whatever you like — it's on me today.
Warm: generously handing over the choice
A: 그냥 제 방식대로 할게요. B: …그래요, 마음대로 하세요.
A: I'll just do it my way. B: …Fine, suit yourself.
Real situation: cold, resigned, passive-aggressive tone
nuance: Means 'do it however you wish,' from 마음 ('mind/heart') + -대로 ('in accordance with') + 하세요 ('please do'), so literally 'act according to your heart.' Crucially, tone is the entire message: said warmly it's open-handed generosity ('go right ahead, no need to ask'); said flatly, with a sigh or clipped delivery, it flips into a frosty 'fine, do what you want, I give up' — the same words, opposite feeling, much like English 'suit yourself.' Compare the friendly cousin 마음껏 ('to your heart's content,' as in 마음껏 드세요): it shares the 마음 root but never carries the cold edge, so when you only mean warm encouragement, 마음껏 is the safer pick. Note too that the casual 마음대로 해 and the -든가 variant (마음대로 하든가, 'do whatever, see if I care') lean pointedly annoyed. Register: 마음대로 하세요 is polite-form, 마음대로 해 casual. Two pitfalls for English speakers: first, because the icy reading is so easy to trigger, be careful aiming it at a senior or using it during any tension — it can land as dismissive or rude even when you meant it kindly. Second, spelling — it's one word 마음대로 (no space before 대로); the contraction 맘대로 is fine in casual chat but too informal for polite or written contexts.

From 마음 ('mind/heart') + -대로 ('in accordance with') + 하세요 ('please do'), so literally 'act according to your heart.'

Two pitfalls: first, because the icy reading is so easy to trigger, be careful aiming it at a senior or using it during any tension — it can land as dismissive or rude even when you meant it kindly. Second, spelling — it's one word 마음대로 (no space before 대로); the contraction 맘대로 is fine in casual chat but too informal for polite or written contexts.

mistakes: Using it casually with a senior or in a tense moment without minding tone. The cold 'fine, whatever' reading triggers easily, so to a superior it can sound dismissive — soften with 편하실 대로 하세요 ('do as suits you') when you mean it warmly.
Spacing it as 마음 대로. -대로 is a particle attached to the noun, so it's one word: 마음대로. And 맘대로 (the 맘 contraction) is fine in casual speech but too informal for formal or written use.

Assuming it always sounds generous. Unlike 마음껏 ('to your heart's content,' always warm), 마음대로 하세요 can read as passive-aggressive depending on delivery — if you only mean encouragement, 마음껏 or 편하신 대로 is safer.
